About: The Hydrogen Spectrum — Every Line Is a Jump

Topic
Atomic physics — hydrogen atom spectra

Every spectral line is a transition between two energy levels of the atom.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Draw your first jump

On the left, the ladder shows the first few hydrogen energy levels. Set ni = 3 and nf = 2 in the controls below to draw the arrow. A line appears on the right at the wavelength that jump emits — in the colour it would actually have.

What colour appeared, and where on the spectrum did it land?

2 · Predict where 4 → 2 lands

4 → 2 is a bigger energy jump than 3 → 2. Does the new line land further into the red, or shift toward the blue?

3 · Build the Balmer series

Now set ni = 4, then 5, then 6, always ending at nf = 2. Watch what happens to the SPACING between successive lines.

The lines crowd together toward a limit near 365 nm rather than spreading out evenly — because the energy LEVELS crowd toward zero. Each line is a level gap, so the pattern of lines is the pattern of gaps.

4 · Predict: where does 2 → 1 land?

All the visible hydrogen lines land on n = 2. What about a jump landing on n = 1 (the Lyman series)? The 2 → 1 gap is much bigger than any Balmer gap. Where should the line fall?

5 · The one thing to notice

Every line in the spectrum is one arrow on the energy ladder. Only the arrows landing on n = 2 happen to be visible; the rest are UV or IR. Try any jump — a 4 → 3 Paschen line lands at 1875 nm in the infrared. Same physics, invisible photon.

The picture the eye sees (a few coloured lines) is a slice of a much larger fingerprint. That fingerprint is the level ladder.

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A hydrogen atom gives out or takes in light only in single photons. The sim draws one jump between two energy levels, and puts the matching photon on a wavelength strip.

What you'll learn

  • How the energy of a hydrogen level depends on its number n.
  • How the two levels of a jump set the photon's energy and wavelength.
  • How jumps are grouped into named series.
  • How to read the strip's ultraviolet, visible and infrared bands.
Two views: a ladder of levels, and a strip where each photon's wavelength lands.

What's on screen

  • Energy ladder (left): one rung for each level n = 1 to 7, with its energy in eV, and an arrow for the jump you pick.
  • Wavelength strip (right): 90 to 2200 nm. A solid line is visible light, a dashed line is invisible.
  • Current jump and Lines drawn panels: the numbers for your jump, and the list of what is drawn.
See itStart with no jump drawn. Watch for: the ladder on the left, and an empty strip with its three bands on the right.

Fixed: the sim uses 13.6057 eV, so its labels read −13.61 eV for n = 1, and hc = 1239.84 eV·nm. The sheet rounds these to 13.6 eV and 1240 eV·nm.

03

Hydrogen's energy levels are Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV

In the Bohr model the electron can sit only on certain levels, numbered by a whole number n = 1, 2, 3, … The sim draws n = 1 to 7. Level n has the energy

Eₙ = −13.6 / n² eV

The minus sign means the electron is bound. E = 0 is an electron just free of the atom, so the ground state, n = 1, needs 13.6 eV to ionise.

As n grows, Eₙ climbs toward 0, and the gap between neighbouring levels shrinks. It is 10.20 eV from n = 1 to n = 2, 1.89 eV from 2 to 3, and 0.31 eV from 4 to 5. That is why the ladder bunches up just under E = 0.

See itLook at the ladder with no jump drawn. Watch for: n = 1 at −13.61 eV far below the rest, and the upper rungs packed together under E = 0.
04

A jump gives one photon whose energy is the whole gap

When the electron drops from level nᵢ to a lower level n_f, the atom gives out one photon. Its energy is the whole difference between the two levels:

Eγ = 13.6 (1/n_f² − 1/nᵢ²) eV

A photon's energy also fixes its wavelength, through Eγ = hc/λ with hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm. A bigger gap therefore gives a shorter wavelength. In wavelength form this is the Rydberg formula, 1/λ = R (1/n_f² − 1/nᵢ²), with R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹.

For the jump 3 → 2 the gap is 1.890 eV, so λ = 1240 / 1.890 ≈ 656 nm. The sim prints 656.1 nm.

See itDraw the jump 3 → 2. Watch for: 1.890 eV and 656.1 nm in the Current jump panel, and a line on the strip at that wavelength.
05

Jumps are named by the level they end on

A series is every jump that ends on the same level n_f. The sim names five: n_f = 1 is Lyman, 2 Balmer, 3 Paschen, 4 Brackett and 5 Pfund. The table gives the first three, using levels n = 1 to 7.

SeriesEnds onLinesWavelengthsRegion
Lymann_f = 16122 to 93 nmultraviolet
Balmern_f = 25656 to 397 nmvisible
Paschenn_f = 341875 to 1005 nminfrared

The strip's bands split at 380 nm and 780 nm. Among these levels only Balmer jumps land between them, so the eye sees only those lines. The sim draws an invisible line dashed.

See itDraw the jump 2 → 1. Watch for: 121.5 nm and a dashed line left of the visible band.
See itDraw the jump 4 → 3. Watch for: 1874.6 nm and a dashed line right of the visible band.
06

Lines crowd toward a series limit

Take the jumps that end on n = 2, from nᵢ = 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. They land at 656.1, 486.0, 433.9, 410.1 and 396.9 nm. The spacing between neighbours falls from 170 to 52, 24 and 13 nm.

The reason is in the levels. The photon energy approaches 13.6 / n_f² eV as nᵢ grows, because the upper levels crowd under E = 0. For n_f = 2 that is 3.40 eV, which is λ = 1240 / 3.40 ≈ 365 nm. This is the series limit, the wavelength for nᵢ → ∞.

Every series has one. The Lyman limit is 91 nm, the Balmer limit 365 nm and the Paschen limit 820 nm. The sim draws a dotted line for it once a series has two lines on the strip.

See itDraw 3 → 2, 4 → 2, 5 → 2 and 6 → 2. Watch for: four Balmer lines bunching up toward the dotted series limit at 365 nm.
07

Absorption and the strip's edge

Choose nᵢ below n_f and the arrow points up. The atom takes in a photon whose energy is exactly the gap. The sim draws it at the same wavelength as the downward jump between those two levels: 2 → 3 and 3 → 2 both give 1.890 eV and 656.1 nm. Only the arrow and the label change, from emit ↓ to absorb ↑.

The sim does not check whether the atom is in the lower level. A real gas absorbs a line only if some atoms start on that level.

The strip stops at 2200 nm. Jumps beyond it, such as 5 → 4 at 4050 nm, are named at the strip's edge instead of drawn. The Current jump panel still gives their true wavelength.

See itDraw the upward jump 2 → 3. Watch for: an upward arrow tagged absorb, and absorb ↑ at 656.1 nm.
See itDraw the jump 5 → 4. Watch for: the strip's note that 5 → 4 lands at 4050 nm, beyond its axis.
08

Where it matters

  • Identifying gases. Each element has its own levels, so its lines are a fingerprint. Astronomers read the hydrogen lines in starlight and glowing clouds to find what an object is made of.
  • The colour of hydrogen gas. A hydrogen discharge glows pinkish red. The glow is the visible Balmer lines blended, led by the red 3 → 2 line at 656 nm.
  • Invisible series. Air absorbs the far ultraviolet, so the Lyman lines are measured in vacuum or from space. Paschen lines need infrared detectors.
  • The formula's history. Balmer and Rydberg fitted formulas to measured lines. Bohr's levels explained why the fit works.
Go deeper

The sim treats the nucleus as infinitely heavy, so it reads 656.1 nm for 3 → 2, against 656.3 nm measured in air. Quantum mechanics keeps the energies Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV to a good approximation, but electrons do not follow orbits, and it splits each level very slightly (fine structure).

09

Summary

In one line. Each jump between two hydrogen levels is an arrow on the ladder and a line on the wavelength strip.

Key points

  • Hydrogen's levels are Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, and they bunch up toward E = 0.
  • A jump's photon carries the whole gap, and Eγ = hc/λ turns it into a wavelength.
  • The final level n_f names the series: Lyman 1, Balmer 2, Paschen 3.
  • An upward jump is absorption, at the same wavelength as the downward one.

Common mix-ups

  • "The lines are evenly spaced." They bunch toward the series limit, because the upper levels bunch.
  • "Only the visible lines are real." The ultraviolet and infrared lines come from the same kind of jump. The eye just cannot see them.
  • "A bigger jump gives a longer wavelength." A bigger gap means a larger photon energy, so a shorter wavelength.

Things to try on your own

  • Set n_f = 2 and step nᵢ from 3 to 7, noting each wavelength in the Current jump panel.
  • Find the jump that gives about 1005 nm.
  • Pick 1 → 2, then 2 → 1, and compare the arrows and the readout.
